print("Shipping rate: $", shipping_rate, sep="")
Closer Look

By default, print() puts a space between its arguments. Here, sep="" removes that separator so the rate appears immediately after the dollar sign. Changing the separator affects the displayed message, not the chosen rate.

We continue to assume that the input is a number greater than zero. As you learned in Week 1, input() returns a string, so float() converts that string to a number and allows a weight such as 1.5. The decision diamond has become the condition weight <= 2, and the two assignments correspond to its paths. The final display statement follows both paths. A weight of 1.5 or 2 produces the lower rate, while a weight of 3 produces the higher rate.

You also met comparison operators in Week 1. A comparison produces True or False; here, that result can determine which path the program follows.

An expression that produces True or False is a Boolean expression. Here, weight <= 2 determines which path runs. Remember that = assigns a value, while == compares values for equality.

10.2 The if Statement and Indentation

An if statement runs one or more statements when its condition is True. Consider a program that displays a message for packages in the lower weight range:

weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))

if weight <= 2:
    print("The lower shipping rate applies.")

print("Thank you for checking our shipping rates.")

For a weight of 1.5, both messages appear. For a weight of 3, the first message is skipped, but the thank-you message still appears.

In Python, the statements controlled by an if form a block. Indentation shows which statements belong to that block. The if header ends with a colon, and every statement in its block is indented beneath it at the same level. Use four spaces for each indentation level.

Returning to the previous indentation level ends the block. A statement at that level is outside the if block. Moving a statement into the block therefore changes when it runs:

weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))

if weight <= 2:
    print("The lower shipping rate applies.")
    print("Thank you for checking our shipping rates.")

Now both messages belong to the if block. For a weight of 3, neither appears. Both versions are valid Python, but their indentation gives them different behaviour.

An if statement on its own either runs its block or skips it. Adding else gives the program an alternative block, as in our shipping calculator:

if weight <= 2:
    shipping_rate = 8
else:
    shipping_rate = 14

Exactly one assignment runs. The else has no condition of its own: it covers every case rejected by the if condition. Its header ends with a colon and aligns with the if to which it belongs.

The display statement belongs after the entire selection because both paths need it. This combines selection with the surrounding sequence of input, processing, and output.

10.3 Choosing Among Several Paths

Now consider a fictional cinema with three ticket prices:

Age Ticket Price
Younger than 13 Child $8
13 through 64 Adult $14
65 or older Senior $10

The customer enters an age, and the program displays the corresponding price. For now, we assume the input is a whole number greater than or equal to zero. We will handle negative ages later in this chapter.

One condition separates two paths. To choose among three prices, we need another condition. The keyword elif means “else if.” Python checks its condition only when the earlier conditions in the same chain were False:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

if age < 13:
    ticket_price = 8
elif age >= 65:
    ticket_price = 10
else:
    ticket_price = 14

print("Ticket price: $", ticket_price, sep="")

Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first matching branch, one of the chain’s alternative paths. For an age of 70, age < 13 is False and age >= 65 is True, so Python assigns the senior price. For an age of 10, the first condition is True, so Python does not check the elif. For an age of 30, both conditions are False, so the else block assigns the adult price.

An if-elif-else chain can contain several elif clauses. The final else is optional, but when present it must come last. Without an else, no branch runs when every condition is False. In this program, the earlier conditions leave ages 13 through 64 for else. The shared display statement then runs after the chain.

Condition order matters when conditions overlap. Consider this incorrect attempt:

if age >= 13:
    ticket_price = 14
elif age >= 65:
    ticket_price = 10
else:
    ticket_price = 8

An age of 70 satisfies age >= 13, so the first branch assigns the adult price. Python never reaches the senior condition. Arrange overlapping conditions so that an earlier branch does not capture a case intended for a later one.

10.4 Combining Conditions

In Week 1, you previewed the Boolean operators and, or, and not: and requires both conditions to be True, or requires at least one of them, and not reverses its condition. We can now use them to combine comparisons in a single condition. We will study Boolean logic in more depth later in the course.

For example, an adult ticket applies when the age is at least 13 and at most 64:

if age >= 13 and age <= 64:
    print("The adult ticket price applies.")

Both comparisons must be True. An age of 30 satisfies both, while an age of 70 fails the second.

For a non-negative age, either the child condition or the senior condition identifies a customer who does not pay the adult price:

if age < 13 or age >= 65:
    print("A child or senior ticket price applies.")

The result is True when either comparison is True. In this example, that means the age is in the child or senior range.

A common mistake is to leave out part of a comparison. To check whether an age is exactly 12 or exactly 65, write each comparison in full:

age == 12 or age == 65

Do not write:

age == 12 or 65

The second expression does not compare age with 65. As a condition, it succeeds for every age; we will see why later in the course.

10.5 Independent and Nested Decisions

An if-elif chain chooses at most one branch. Separate if statements make independent decisions, so more than one block can run.

Suppose the cinema displays one message for a child ticket and another for a booking of five or more tickets:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
ticket_count = int(input("How many tickets are you buying? "))

if age < 13:
    print("A child ticket is needed for this customer.")

if ticket_count >= 5:
    print("Please collect this booking at the group counter.")

For an age of 10 and a ticket count of 5, both messages appear. Changing the second if to elif would make Python skip the ticket-count check whenever the child condition was True. Use separate if statements when both actions may occur. Use an elif chain when the branches are alternatives.

A nested decision places one decision inside another decision’s block. This is useful when the inner decision should happen only on a particular outer path.

We can use nesting to check whether an age is valid before choosing a ticket price. The first decision separates invalid ages from valid ones. Ticket selection happens only on the valid path, so it is nested inside that path. Here is that design expressed in Python:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

if age < 0:
    print("Age must be zero or greater.")
else:
    if age < 13:
        ticket_price = 8
    elif age >= 65:
        ticket_price = 10
    else:
        ticket_price = 14

    print("Ticket price: $", ticket_price, sep="")

The outer decision checks whether the age is negative. If it is, the program displays an error; otherwise, the inner selection chooses the ticket price. Its headers are indented four spaces, and their blocks are indented eight spaces. The final print() returns to four spaces, so it follows the inner selection but remains inside the outer else. A negative age therefore never reaches the price display.

This program checks one input and then ends. Asking again after an error will require a loop; Chapter 9 represented that repetition with a loop-back arrow. The program also assumes that int() can convert the input. We will handle failed conversions separately.

10.6 Testing Decision Paths

Testing compares what a program does with what it should do. Debugging finds and fixes the cause when those results differ.

In Chapter 9, we checked a design by following a path through its flowchart. Now we can run the Python program with chosen inputs and compare the displayed results with the cinema’s rules.

For the version that checks negative ages, predict the expected output for each age below before reading the table’s second column:

Age Expected output Why this case helps
-1 Age must be zero or greater. Just below the accepted range
0 Ticket price: $8 Lowest accepted age
12 Ticket price: $8 Last age in the child range
13 Ticket price: $14 First age in the adult range
64 Ticket price: $14 Last age in the adult range
65 Ticket price: $10 First age in the senior range

These boundary cases sit at or beside the points where behaviour changes. They help expose mistakes such as using <= where < was intended.

Ordinary values such as 10, 30, and 70 are also useful because they exercise each price branch. Passing these tests provides evidence that the program follows the requirements, although a finite set of tests cannot cover every possible input.

Choose the expected result from the requirements before running the program. Otherwise, it is easy to accept the program’s answer simply because it produced one.

When a result differs from what you expected, trace that input through the code. Check:

  • The conditions: do the comparisons include the correct boundaries?
  • The branch order: does an earlier condition capture the input unexpectedly?
  • The indentation: does each statement belong to the intended path?

For independent decisions, include cases where both conditions are True, only one is True, and neither is True. This can reveal an accidental change from two if statements to an if-elif chain.

10.7 Summary

Selection chooses which statements run for a given input. An if statement can run or skip a block, else provides an alternative, and elif extends the choice to more paths. Indentation defines the blocks, and a chain runs only its first matching branch.

Boolean operators combine conditions. Separate decisions allow multiple actions, while nesting makes one decision depend on another. Test each path and the values where behaviour changes, using the requirements to determine the expected results.

10.8 References and Further Reading

  • Python Tutorial: if Statements: examples of if, elif, and else.
  • Python Language Reference: The if Statement: the formal structure and execution rules for selection.
  • PEP 8: Style Guide for Python Code: conventions for indentation and naming.
  • Beej’s Guide to Python Programming, chapter 6: flow control, Boolean expressions, and the if statement.

11 Working with Strings

So far, we have used strings mainly to read input and display messages. Working more closely with text requires us to look inside those values. A string is an ordered sequence of characters: we can find its length, select a character by its position, and examine the text it contains.

We can also combine strings, adjust capitalization, remove surrounding spaces, and insert calculated values into messages. These operations produce new values without changing the original string. Understanding that distinction will help us use strings correctly as our programs become more involved.

11.1 Strings and String Literals

Chapter 6 introduced string literals, and Chapter 7 introduced str as the type used for strings. We can now distinguish the notation written in code from the value it produces.

A string literal is the quoted notation used to write a string value directly in source code. The surrounding quotes mark the literal’s boundaries; they are not part of the value.

>>> "COMP 1510"
'COMP 1510'
>>> 'hello'
'hello'
Closer Look

The REPL uses quotes to show that a result is a string, and may choose a different quote style from your literal. print() displays the string’s contents without those surrounding quotes, so the same value can look different in the two displays.

You can use single or double quotes. Choosing the outer quotes lets you include the other kind inside the text:

print("It's easy")
print('She said "hi"')

The empty string, written "", contains no characters. It is still a string, just as zero is still a number.

11.2 Escape Sequences

Some characters affect how text is displayed. A newline moves text to the next line, and a tab adds horizontal spacing. Python writes these characters inside a literal with an escape sequence: a backslash followed by a character with a special meaning. For example, \n represents one newline character.

Escape sequence Meaning
\n Newline: moves output to the next line
\t Tab
\\ A single backslash
\' A single quote
\" A double quote 
print("Line one\nLine two")
print("Name:\tAda")

The first statement displays its text on two lines. The second inserts a tab between Name: and Ada. Although \n is written with two characters in the source code, it represents one newline character in the string.

Often, choosing the other quote style is easier than using an escape. For example, the apostrophe in "It's easy" does not need to be escaped because the string literal uses double quotes.

11.3 Characters, Length, and Indexes

Each letter, digit, space, or punctuation mark in a string counts as one character. The built-in len() function returns the number of characters.

Each character sits at a numbered position called an index. Python numbers indexes from zero:

The string "Python" contains six characters, with indexes from 0 through 5. In a non-empty string, the first index is 0 and the final non-negative index is one less than the length.

Square brackets after a string select the character at an index:

>>> word = "Python"
>>> len(word)
6
>>> word[0]
'P'
>>> word[1]
'y'
>>> word[len(word) - 1]
'n'

Asking for an index outside the string raises an IndexError. The valid indexes of this six-character string run from 0 to 5, so word[6] fails.

The expression len(word) - 1 calculates the final index without assuming a particular string length. When text comes from input, we must first check that it contains at least one character:

name = input("Name: ")

if len(name) > 0:
    print("The first character is", name[0])
    print("The final character is", name[len(name) - 1])
else:
    print("No name was entered.")

The condition protects both indexing expressions. An empty string has length 0 and has no valid indexes, so trying name[0] without checking would raise an IndexError.

Negative indexes count from the end of a string. The index -1 refers to the final character:

>>> word[-1]
'n'

Python can also extract several characters at once. We will study that operation, called slicing, alongside lists later in the course.

11.4 Strings Are Immutable

Selecting a character does not mean that you can replace it. This assignment fails:

>>> word[0] = "J"

Python raises a TypeError. Strings are immutable, which means that an existing string value cannot be changed in place.

If a string cannot be changed in place, how can a program produce different text? A method is a function that belongs to a value, and strings provide many of them. Some methods return a new string while leaving the original unchanged.

You have already seen calls such as len(course), where the value goes inside the parentheses. A method call uses a different form: course.upper(). Here, course refers to a string, the dot connects it to the method named upper, and the parentheses call that method. The call returns an uppercase version of the string, which you can assign to a name:

course = "Introduction to Programming"
uppercase_course = course.upper()

print(course)            # Introduction to Programming
print(uppercase_course)  # INTRODUCTION TO PROGRAMMING

You can also assign the result back to the same name:

course = course.upper()

This does not change the original string. It makes course refer to the new string.

This difference explains a common surprise:

>>> name = "Ada"
>>> name.upper()
'ADA'
>>> name
'Ada'

The method produces a result, but this example does not store it. If the program needs the uppercase value later, it must assign the result to a name:

>>> uppercase_name = name.upper()
>>> uppercase_name
'ADA'

The same principle applies throughout this chapter: an operation can inspect a string or produce another value, but it does not edit the original string.

11.5 Combining Strings

Joining strings is concatenation. Python uses the + operator for it:

>>> first = "COMP"
>>> course = first + " 1510"
>>> course
'COMP 1510'

The * operator repeats a string a whole number of times:

>>> "ha" * 3
'hahaha'

The + operator cannot directly combine a string and a number. Although str() can convert a number first, f-strings are usually a clearer way to mix text with values.

11.6 A Few Useful String Methods

We have already used upper() to produce uppercase text. Here are six useful string methods. In the table, s is the string being used and t is the text to search for:

Method Result
s.upper() A new string with each letter uppercase
s.lower() A new string with each letter lowercase
s.isupper() True if the string has at least one letter and all its letters are uppercase
s.islower() True if the string has at least one letter and all its letters are lowercase
s.strip() A new string with surrounding whitespace removed
s.find(t) The index of the first occurrence of t, or -1 if it is absent 
>>> course = "  Comp 1510  "
>>> course.strip()
'Comp 1510'
>>> course.lower()
'  comp 1510  '
>>> "COMP 1510".isupper()
True
>>> "comp 1510".islower()
True
>>> "Comp 1510".islower()
False
>>> "COMP 1510".find("M")
2
>>> "COMP 1510".find("z")
-1

These methods leave the original string unchanged, but their results have different types. upper(), lower(), and strip() return strings; isupper() and islower() return True or False; find() returns an integer position, or -1 when the text is absent. That -1 reports a failed search; it does not mean that a match was found at the final character.

strip() removes whitespace from the beginning and end, including spaces and tabs. It leaves spaces inside the text intact, so " Comp 1510 ".strip() preserves the space between Comp and 1510.

What a method returns determines how you can use it. A method that returns a string can provide cleaned or normalized text:

name = input("Name: ")
name = name.strip()
print("Hello,", name)

Methods are also useful in conditions. Converting text to lowercase before comparing it lets the program accept several capitalizations:

answer = input("Continue? ")
answer = answer.strip()
answer = answer.lower()

if answer == "yes":
    print("Continuing")
else:
    print("Stopping")

First, strip() removes surrounding whitespace. Then lower() produces lowercase text, allowing "yes", "YES", and " Yes " to satisfy the same condition. Each assignment makes answer refer to the next result.

Python provides many more string methods. You do not need to memorize a large list. Learn a small useful set now, and consult the string methods documentation when a program needs something else.

11.7 Formatting Output with F-Strings

An f-string is a string literal prefixed with f. Expressions inside braces are evaluated and placed into the text:

>>> name = "Ada"
>>> age = 19
>>> f"{name} is {age} years old"
'Ada is 19 years old'
>>> f"Age next year: {age + 1}"
'Age next year: 20'

The braces can contain a variable or another expression that produces a value.

Compare two ways to display the same result:

name = "Ada"
score = 92

print(name, "scored", score)
print(f"{name} scored {score}")

Both statements work. The f-string keeps the spaces and wording together, making the intended output easier to see in the program.

A colon after an expression introduces a format specification. Writing :.2f displays a number with exactly two digits after the decimal point, rounding the displayed value when needed:

>>> shipping_rate = 8
>>> f"Shipping rate: ${shipping_rate:.2f}"
'Shipping rate: $8.00'

Formatting changes the text produced for display; it does not change the value stored in the variable.

Here is the shipping calculator from Chapter 10 with its output formatted using f-strings. As before, this version assumes the user enters a positive numeric weight:

weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))

if weight <= 2:
    shipping_rate = 8
else:
    shipping_rate = 14

print("COMP Couriers")
print(f"Weight: {weight} kg")
print(f"Shipping rate: ${shipping_rate:.2f}")

Use f-strings when output combines text with values. They keep the output pattern readable and give you control over how numbers appear.

F-strings create strings; they do not print by themselves. In the REPL, Python displays the resulting value, but a program normally passes the f-string to print() or assigns it to a name:

customer = "Ada"
message = f"Welcome, {customer}!"
print(message)

This prints Welcome, Ada!. Building a string and displaying it are separate operations, even when a program performs them in the same statement.

11.8 Summary

A string is an immutable sequence of characters. A string literal is text written directly in source code to create a string value. len() returns the number of characters, and an index selects one character from the sequence.

Strings cannot be changed in place, but expressions and methods can produce new strings. The methods upper(), lower(), and strip() return new strings, while find() returns an integer index. An f-string places the values of expressions into text, and :.2f displays a number with two digits after the decimal point.

11.9 References and Further Reading

  • String methods: the complete list of methods supported by strings.
  • F-strings in the language reference: the formal syntax of formatted string literals.
  • Beej’s Guide to Python Programming, chapter 7: strings, immutability, and f-string formatting.

12 Using Python Modules

Python programs often use code that is already available. You have called built-in functions such as input() to read text, int() to convert a value, and print() to display it. Python also includes a standard library of reusable tools.

A module groups related functions and values. To use functions from a module such as math, you first import it. We will use math and random to see how to access their tools and use the results in calculations.

12.1 Importing a Module

The import statement makes a module available under its name. Imports normally appear at the top of the file, before the statements that use them. This example uses math.sqrt() to calculate a square root:

import math

number = float(input("Enter a non-negative number: "))
root = math.sqrt(number)
print(f"Square root: {root:.2f}")

The expression math.sqrt(number) uses dot notation: math identifies the module, sqrt selects its square-root function, and the parentheses call that function with number.

The example assumes that the user enters a number greater than or equal to zero. The prompt describes the expected input; it does not check it. We will add input checks when we study loops.

The dot also appeared with string methods in Chapter 11. The name before the dot tells you where the operation comes from:

  • name.upper() calls a method on the string referred to by name.
  • math.sqrt(25) calls a function provided by the imported math module.

After import math, write math.sqrt(25); the import does not create a separate name called sqrt.

12.2 The math Module

The math module contains mathematical functions and constants. We will use two of them here:

Name Purpose Example
math.sqrt(x) Returns the square root of x math.sqrt(25) produces 5.0
math.pi Python’s floating-point approximation of π\piπ Approximately 3.141592653589793

math.pi is a value, so it is used without parentheses. math.sqrt is a function, so parentheses call it:

>>> import math
>>> math.pi
3.141592653589793
>>> math.sqrt(81)
9.0

12.2.1 Calculating the Area of a Circle

For a circle with radius rrr, the area is A=πr2A = \pi r^2A=πr2. This program uses math.pi for π\piπ and assumes the user enters a positive numeric radius:

import math

radius = float(input("Enter the circle radius: "))
area = math.pi * radius ** 2
print(f"Area: {area:.2f}")

Python squares radius with ** 2 and multiplies the result by math.pi. The f-string displays two decimal places without changing the value stored in area.

12.2.2 Calculating Distance with math.sqrt()

Suppose two points are 3 units apart horizontally and 4 units apart vertically. By the Pythagorean theorem, the distance between them is 32+42=5\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 532+42​=5. The program first stores the sum of the squares in squared_distance, then passes that value to math.sqrt():

import math

horizontal = 3
vertical = 4
squared_distance = horizontal ** 2 + vertical ** 2
distance = math.sqrt(squared_distance)

print(f"Distance: {distance:.2f}")

horizontal and vertical are starting values. squared_distance is an intermediate variable holding 25. math.sqrt() returns 5.0, which is assigned to distance and displayed. You could pass the sum directly as math.sqrt(horizontal ** 2 + vertical ** 2); the name lets you inspect it.

12.3 The random Module

The random module provides randint(a, b) for choosing an integer between two limits:

>>> import random
>>> random.randint(1, 6)
4
>>> random.randint(1, 6)
1
Reading The Output

The numbers above are sample results, not output your calls must match. A repeated roll can return the same number; that alone does not mean the program is stuck.

Both limits are included, so random.randint(1, 6) can return any integer from 1 through 6, like a six-sided die. The limits must be integers, and the first must not exceed the second.

12.3.1 Choosing a Random Point

A program can import more than one module. This example chooses a point at random and calculates its distance from the origin:

import math
import random

x = random.randint(-5, 5)
y = random.randint(-5, 5)
distance = math.sqrt(x ** 2 + y ** 2)

print(f"Point: ({x}, {y})")
print(f"Distance from the origin: {distance:.2f}")

The names before the dots identify which module supplies each function. Two calls to random.randint() choose the point’s x and y coordinates; math.sqrt() uses them to calculate the distance. A later run may choose a different point, or the same one again.

When you need more from a module, check its documentation for available functions, the arguments they take, and the values they return.

12.4 Summary

The standard library is ready-made code that comes with Python. An import statement makes a module available, and dot notation selects a function or value from that module.

The math module provides math.sqrt() and the value math.pi. The random module provides random.randint(a, b), which returns a whole number from the inclusive range a through b. Keeping the module name visible makes the source of each library tool clear.

12.5 References and Further Reading

  • The Python Standard Library: the official index of modules that ship with Python.
  • math: Mathematical functions
  • random: Generate pseudo-random numbers
  • Beej’s Guide to Python Programming, chapter 12: importing and using modules.

13 Repetition in Python

A program often needs to perform the same work more than once. It might ask again after invalid input, examine each character in a string, or keep a running total. Writing a separate statement for every repetition becomes impractical when the input determines how many are needed.

A loop lets us write the repeated steps once and control how often they run. Chapter 9 showed this idea with a loop-back arrow in a flowchart. We will now express it in Python using while and for.

13.1 From Repeated Statements to Loops

Suppose a program needs to display the numbers from one through five. One approach is to write five separate statements:

print(1)
print(2)
print(3)
print(4)
print(5)

This works, but the program describes every repetition separately. Extending it to one hundred would require ninety-five more statements. If the counting rule changed, many lines might need to change with it.

The repeated lines can be replaced by a rule: display the current number, increase it, and stop after five. One pass through a loop’s block is an iteration.

Before writing a loop, answer three questions:

  1. What values, if any, must be set before the repetition begins?
  2. Which statements need to run during each iteration?
  3. What will change from one iteration to the next, and how will the loop know when to stop?

Python provides two loop statements. A while loop repeats as long as a Boolean condition is True. A for loop takes items from a sequence one at a time; in this chapter, the sequence will be a string. We will begin with while because its condition makes the decision to repeat or stop explicit.

13.2 The while Statement

The while loop repeats its block while its condition is True. This loop counts from one to five:

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

Three parts make this loop work:

  1. Before the loop, count is initialized to 1.
  2. At the top of every pass, Python tests count <= 5. If it is True, the indented block runs. If it is False, the loop ends.
  3. The statement count += 1 increases count by one before the next condition check.

Trace each condition check to see how count changes and why the loop stops:

Condition check count at the test count <= 5 Output
1 1 True 1
2 2 True 2
3 3 True 3
4 4 True 4
5 5 True 5
6 6 False No output

Python checks the condition six times, but the body runs only five times. At the final check, count is 6, so count <= 5 is False and no sixth iteration begins.

The condition is tested before every pass, including the first. If it is False immediately, the body does not run. A while loop therefore runs its body zero or more times.

The flowchart below shows the two possible paths after a condition check:

In the counting example above, the diamond represents count <= 5 and the loop body contains print(count) and count += 1. After both statements run, execution returns to the condition for another check. The False path leaves the loop without running its body.

Indentation determines which statements repeat. Adding a statement after the loop makes the difference visible:

count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(count)
    count += 1
print("Done")

Both indented statements belong to the loop, so both repeat. print("Done") is dedented, which ends the loop’s block. It runs once, after the condition becomes False.

Chapter 10 used boundary cases to check selection. Loop boundaries require the same care: predict what the loop just above would print if you changed count <= 3 to count < 3, then check yourself in the REPL. Getting a boundary like this wrong causes an off-by-one error, where a loop repeats once too often or once too few.

13.2.1 Avoiding Infinite Loops

If nothing in a loop changes the condition, the loop may never stop:

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)

An infinite loop keeps repeating without ending on its own. Here, count never changes, so count <= 5 remains True and the program repeatedly prints 1. Press Ctrl-C in the terminal to interrupt a program stuck in a loop.

An update can be present and still move in the wrong direction:

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count -= 1

After the first iteration, count becomes 0, then -1, then -2. All these values are still less than or equal to 5, so the condition never becomes False. The starting value, condition, and update must work together for a counting loop to stop.

A Useful Habit

Before running a counting loop, trace its starting value through two updates and check the condition each time. If the values move away from the stopping point, fix the update first.

13.2.2 Validating Input with while and break

Chapter 9’s shipping flowchart keeps asking for a package weight until the weight is positive. We can now express that behaviour in Python by reading and checking a new weight inside a loop.

For this task, the decision to stop comes after reading the input. We use while True to keep the loop running while we read and check each weight. Its condition is always True, so it cannot become False and end the loop.

To end the loop after a successful check, we use the break statement. When Python reaches break, it leaves the loop immediately. Placing break inside if weight > 0: lets a positive weight end the repetition.

As before, assume the input can be converted to a number. The loop checks whether it is positive; handling text that cannot be converted comes later.

The input statement runs at the start of every iteration:

while True:
    weight = float(input("Enter the package weight in kilograms: "))
    if weight > 0:
        break
    print("Weight must be positive.")

if weight <= 2:
    shipping_rate = 8
else:
    shipping_rate = 14

print(f"Shipping rate: ${shipping_rate:.2f}")

Suppose the user enters 0, then -2, then 1.5. Trace the decision after each input:

Value entered weight > 0 What happens next
0 False Display the error and ask again
-2 False Display the error and ask again
1.5 True Run break and leave the loop

After break, execution continues with if weight <= 2:. The program can now choose a shipping rate using the accepted weight.

The same pattern applies to other inputs:

  1. Start a while True loop and read a value inside it.
  2. If the value is valid, use break to leave the loop.
  3. Otherwise, explain the problem and let the next iteration ask again.

13.3 The for Statement

Suppose you want to display every character in a string. A for loop visits the characters one at a time, so you can describe what to do with each one:

course = "COMP"
for letter in course:
    print(letter)

Read the header as “for each letter in course.” Here, letter is the loop variable. On each iteration, Python automatically assigns the next character to it and runs the indented block. When there are no characters left, the loop ends.

Iteration Value of letter Output
1 "C" C
2 "O" O
3 "M" M
4 "P" P

An empty string contains no characters, so a for loop over "" runs zero times. A one-character string produces exactly one iteration.

As with while, the header ends with a colon and the loop’s block is indented. Use a singular name such as letter for the loop variable because it refers to one character at a time.

A for loop can contain more than one statement:

word = "Code"
for letter in word:
    print(letter)
    print(letter.lower())
print("Done")

Both indented statements run for each character. print("Done") is outside the loop, so it runs once after the final character.

A condition inside the loop can choose how to handle each character:

course = "COMP 1510"

for character in course:
    if character == " ":
        print("space")
    else:
        print(character)

The loop still visits every character, including the space. The if statement chooses which print() call runs during each iteration.

13.4 A Simple Accumulator

The previous for examples display something during each iteration. You can also use a loop to build one result and display it after the loop finishes.

An accumulator is a variable initialized before a loop and updated inside it to build a running result. This example counts lowercase "a" characters in a word:

word = "banana"
count = 0

for letter in word:
    if letter == "a":
        count += 1

print(count)

In the earlier while loop, count controlled when repetition stopped. Here, it begins at 0 and increases for each matching letter; its final value is the result.

Each statement has a deliberate position. Initialization belongs before the loop; placing count = 0 inside the loop would erase the earlier work on every iteration. The update belongs inside the if because only a matching character should increase the count. The final print(count) belongs after the loop because the program should report the completed result once.

Trace the value carefully:

letter letter == "a" count after the iteration
"b" False 0
"a" True 1
"n" False 1
"a" True 2
"n" False 2
"a" True 3

The loop checks every letter, while the if statement changes count only for a match.

The comparison matches lowercase "a" only. Convert the input to lowercase first to count uppercase and lowercase forms:

word = input("Word: ")
word = word.lower()
count = 0

for letter in word:
    if letter == "a":
        count += 1

print(f"The word contains the letter a {count} times.")

The counting loop is unchanged; the program now reads and lowercases the word first.

13.5 Tracing Loops by Hand

Chapters 9 and 10 showed how to trace a flowchart or a decision with a chosen input. The tables above use the same technique to follow loops. When you trace a loop yourself, record the small set of values that change. For a while loop, record its condition and changing value; if it uses break, record when that statement runs. For a for loop, record the current character and any accumulator.

A useful trace does not need to reproduce every line of the program. It only needs enough information to answer three questions:

  1. What value controls or advances the loop?
  2. What changes during this iteration?
  3. What must eventually cause the loop to stop?

For a while loop, pay particular attention to the first pass and the condition check or break that ends it. For a for loop, follow the first and last items, and consider what happens with an empty string. These cases help reveal incorrect initial values, comparisons, and updates.

13.6 Choosing Between while and for

Use for when you need to work through the items in a sequence. To count the "a" characters in a word, you need to examine every character, so for is a natural choice.

Use while when you need to repeat an action based on a condition or until a decision inside the loop tells you to stop. To get a positive package weight, the program asks on each pass and uses break when the weight is valid. The values the user enters determine how many times the loop repeats.

13.7 Summary

A loop repeats an indented block. A while loop checks its condition before each pass. It stops when the condition becomes False or a break statement ends it. Input validation can use while True to ask again until the value is valid.

A for loop visits a string’s characters one at a time; its loop variable holds each character in turn. An accumulator starts before a loop and builds a running result inside it.

13.8 References and Further Reading

  • Python Language Reference: The while statement
  • Python Language Reference: The break statement
  • Python Language Reference: The for statement
  • Beej’s Guide to Python Programming, chapter 6: while loops, for loops, and choosing between them.

14 Functions

Quote

“Simplicity is a great virtue but it requires hard work to achieve it and education to appreciate it.”

Edsger W. Dijkstra, On the Nature of Computing Science (EWD 896).

You can now write programs that make decisions and repeat steps. As those programs grow, keeping every step in one long sequence makes it harder to see how the pieces fit together. Functions let you give a name to a particular job, then use that name wherever the program needs the job done.

You already work this way when you call len(word) or random.randint(1, 6): you supply the information a function needs and use the result without writing its steps yourself. You will now define your own functions. You will begin with a function that displays a greeting, then write functions that receive values, calculate results, and work together.

As you read, follow the information through each call: what goes into the function, what happens inside it, and what comes back. That same pattern will help you understand both a short calculation and a program built from several functions.

14.1 Defining and Calling a Function

To display a welcome message at several points in a program, put that job in a function, a reusable block of code. Write a function definition using def, a descriptive name, parentheses, and a colon:

def display_welcome():
    print("Welcome!")

display_welcome()
display_welcome()

The indented statement is the function’s body. Defining the function makes it available, but does not run it. Each display_welcome() is a function call: Python runs the body, then continues after the call. Two calls display the message twice.

A call placed above the definition stops the program, because the name does not exist until the def runs:

NameError: name 'display_welcome' is not defined

Python simply has not reached the definition yet. Keep definitions above the calls that use them.

To personalize the greeting, the function needs to receive a name. A parameter is a name in the definition that receives a value when the function is called:

def display_greeting(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

display_greeting("Maya")
display_greeting("Sam")

Each call supplies an argument, a value passed to the function. The parameter name receives "Maya" for the first call and "Sam" for the second. The body stays the same while the supplied value changes.

To display a person’s name alongside a message, give the function two parameters. Arguments are matched to parameters by position:

def display_message(name, message):
    print(f"{name}: {message}")

student_name = "Maya"
display_message(student_name, "Ready to begin")

Here, name receives the value of student_name, and message receives "Ready to begin". The calling code’s variable and the function’s parameter do not need matching names.

These definitions require one argument per parameter. If one is missing, Python stops with a TypeError, and the message names the parameter that received nothing:

TypeError: display_message() missing 1 required positional argument: 'message'

Choose names that describe the job, as display_welcome, display_greeting, and display_message do here. A reader should understand what a call does without opening its definition.

A Useful Habit

When checking a function, change one argument at a time. For display_message(), try another message for the same person, then another person with the same message. Each argument should move one part of the output and nothing else: an argument that changes nothing is probably unused, and an effect in the wrong place usually means the arguments are swapped.

14.2 Returning a Value

Displaying a greeting finishes that function’s job. Other functions produce values that you can store or use in further calculations, such as a duration converted from minutes to seconds.

The return statement sends a return value back to the caller, the code that made the call. The caller can store that value or use it as part of an expression:

def minutes_to_seconds(minutes):
    return minutes * 60

seconds = minutes_to_seconds(3)
print(seconds)
print(minutes_to_seconds(3) + 30)

Assigning the result of minutes_to_seconds(3) to seconds stores 180 for later use. In the final line, the same call is part of a larger calculation that produces 210. Change the argument to 5 in both calls and predict the results before running them.

A function can have more than one return. You can use the selection statements you already know to choose what to return. This function selects the longer of two words, choosing the first when their lengths are equal:

def longer_word(first, second):
    if len(first) >= len(second):
        return first
    return second

print(longer_word("sun", "planet"))
print(longer_word("tree", "moon"))

Executing return ends that call immediately. When the condition is true, Python returns first without reaching the final statement. Otherwise, it returns second. Putting the final return in an else branch is also valid; leaving out else here is a style choice.

14.3 Printing Is Not Returning

When a function displays the answer you expected, it is easy to assume that the caller received that answer too. But displaying a value and passing it back are separate actions: print() produces output for a person, while return supplies a value to the calling code. To see the difference, assign the result of a function that only prints its calculation:

def display_seconds(minutes):
    print(minutes * 60)

result = display_seconds(3)
print(f"Stored result: {result}")

Although 180 appears on screen, the assignment receives None, the special value used here to indicate no useful result. The final line therefore displays Stored result: None.

Python returns None whenever a call reaches the end without executing a return. A bare return, with no expression after it, also ends the call and returns None.

Printed output and returned values can look the same in the REPL. These two functions both make 180 appear:

>>> def minutes_to_seconds(minutes):
...     return minutes * 60
...
>>> def display_seconds(minutes):
...     print(minutes * 60)
...
>>> minutes_to_seconds(3)
180
>>> display_seconds(3)
180

The REPL echoes the first call’s returned 180. The second call prints 180 and returns None, which the REPL does not echo. Storing and displaying the result, as the first program in this section does, reveals what the caller received.

Try It Yourself

In the first program in this section, compare displaying the calculation with returning it to the caller:

  1. Add print(result + 30) as a new last line. Predict what it displays, then run the program. If an error occurs, look at the two types it names.
  2. Replace print(minutes * 60) with return minutes * 60. Predict the output again, then run it and compare with the first run.

14.3.1 Returning on Every Path

Checking that a function contains a return is not enough. If selection allows a call to reach the end without executing that statement, the caller still receives None. Consider this unfinished version of longer_word(), which is meant to follow the same rule as before:

def longer_word(first, second):
    if len(first) >= len(second):
        return first

print(longer_word("planet", "sun"))
Try It Yourself

Try the unfinished longer_word() with a different pair of words:

  1. Change the arguments so the second word is longer. Predict the result, then run the program.
  2. Add the missing return so the function returns a word on both paths.
  3. Run it with the first word longer, the second word longer, and two different words of equal length. Check the displayed word each time.

14.4 Documenting a Function

Once a function has a clear job, you should be able to explain how to use it without walking through its code. Someone calling minutes_to_seconds() needs to know what values it accepts and what its result means. A docstring records that information inside the function, where both readers and Python’s help tools can find it.

Place the docstring as the first statement in the body, enclosed in triple quotation marks. Write one short sentence for the job. Add :param and :return: entries only when the inputs or the result need explanation, such as a unit or a limit on the values:

def minutes_to_seconds(minutes):
    """
    Convert a duration in minutes to seconds.

    :param minutes: a non-negative number of minutes
    :return: the equivalent duration in seconds
    """
    return minutes * 60

print(minutes_to_seconds(3))

From the docstring, you can tell which units the function accepts and returns. Its first line alone carries most of that explanation; the entries help when a reader could misunderstand a unit or an input limit. The docstring does not enforce the expectation: negative arguments still produce negative results. Input checks require executable code.

14.4.1 Reading Docstrings

The built-in help() function displays a function’s name, parameters, and docstring. A file can carry a docstring too: a module docstring is a triple-quoted string placed as the first statement in the file to describe its purpose. Calling help() on an imported module displays that description along with information about its functions.

Try It Yourself

Make a docstring visible through Python’s help tool:

  1. Use the complete longer_word() example in the Returning a Value section. Add a short docstring as the first statement in the function, describing the result and which word it returns when the lengths are equal.
  2. Add help(longer_word) as the program’s last line and run it. Look for your docstring beneath the function’s name and parameters.

14.5 Functions That Answer Questions

So far, your functions have returned numbers and strings. A function can also answer a question, such as whether some text is long enough. Giving that check a name lets you use it wherever the program needs to make the same decision.

A predicate function answers a yes-or-no question by returning True or False. longer_word() chose between two values with an if. Since a comparison already produces a Boolean value, you can return it directly. Names beginning with is_ or has_ make the call itself read like the question:

def has_minimum_length(text, minimum):
    return len(text) >= minimum

print(has_minimum_length("hello", 5))
if has_minimum_length("hello", 5):
    print("The text is long enough.")

has_minimum_length("hello", 5) returns True, which you can display with print() or use directly as an if condition. Adding == True compares True with True, or False with False, and changes nothing.

14.6 Using Loops Inside Functions

In Chapter 13, you used an accumulator to count matching characters. You can put that same pattern inside a function so the caller supplies the text and receives the completed count. Here, the function counts spaces:

def count_spaces(text):
    count = 0
    for character in text:
        if character == " ":
            count += 1
    return count

print(count_spaces("one two three"))
print(count_spaces("word"))
print(count_spaces(""))

Each call starts with count = 0, so it does not carry over the previous call’s count. The return sits after the loop because the function must examine every character before the total is ready. An empty string still returns 0: the loop runs zero times, but execution reaches the return.

Try It Yourself

What changes when you move return inside the loop?

  1. Run the example above, then indent return count to line up with if.
  2. Predict the three new results, then run it. Which calls reach return count, and after how many characters?

This is also where return differs from break: inside a function, break ends only the loop it sits in, while return ends the whole call, even from inside a loop.

14.7 Decomposing a Program

In Chapter 9, you used decomposition to plan a solution as a series of smaller steps. Functions now let you organize the code around those jobs. Look for steps that serve one clear purpose, then consider what information that job needs and what result it should produce. These choices give each function a responsibility and define how it works with its callers.

Preparing a duration message involves two jobs: converting minutes to seconds and building the text. Keeping the conversion separate lets other code use its numeric result:

def minutes_to_seconds(minutes):
    return minutes * 60

def duration_message(minutes):
    seconds = minutes_to_seconds(minutes)
    return f"Duration: {seconds} seconds"

print(duration_message(3))

To build the message, duration_message() calls minutes_to_seconds(). The conversion returns 180, which the message function uses to build and return "Duration: 180 seconds". The outer print() displays that string. Arguments carry information into each job, and return values carry the results back to its caller.

Here, minutes_to_seconds() acts as a helper function: it handles a smaller job that duration_message() needs.

Separating these responsibilities gives each function a reason to exist. The conversion can serve another calculation without producing a message, and the message wording can change without changing the conversion. Because both functions return their results, the caller decides whether to display, store, or use them in further work.

14.8 Running and Importing a File

You have used functions from math and random by importing those modules. Your own Python file can also act as a module, allowing another program to use its functions. For example, the duration conversion can be useful even when a program does not need a duration message.

During the first import in a running program, Python executes the file’s statements from top to bottom. Each def makes a function available without running its body. In the previous example, the final print(duration_message(3)) call would also run, displaying a message even if the importing program only wanted the conversion.

14.8.1 Why the Main Guard Matters

A main function, conventionally named main(), gathers the work needed to run the program into one place. It gives you one call to control. A main guard makes that call only when the file is run directly, so importing the file does not start that work.

In durations.py below, main() coordinates the duration program, and the final if statement controls its call:

def minutes_to_seconds(minutes):
    return minutes * 60

def duration_message(minutes):
    seconds = minutes_to_seconds(minutes)
    return f"Duration: {seconds} seconds"

def main():
    minutes = 3
    message = duration_message(minutes)
    print(message)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The guard tests __name__, which Python sets according to how the file is used. When you run durations.py directly, its value is "__main__". The condition is True, so main() runs and displays Duration: 180 seconds.

When another program imports durations, the module’s __name__ is "durations". The condition is False, so Python skips the call to main(). Its functions are still available to the importing program. A file named use_duration.py in the same folder can use the conversion like this:

import durations

print(durations.minutes_to_seconds(2))

This program displays:

120

The call uses the same dot notation as math.sqrt(25): durations names the module, and minutes_to_seconds names its function. The returned value goes to this caller, which displays it with print().

The guard controls only the call indented beneath it. A print() outside the functions and the guard would still run during import. Keeping the program’s starting work inside main() lets the importing program choose which functions to call and how to use their results.

Try It Yourself

Compare the guard’s effect on running and importing durations.py:

  1. Predict the output of both durations.py and use_duration.py if the guard is replaced by an unindented main() call.
  2. Make that change and run both files. Which output changes, and why?

14.9 Reassigning a Parameter

Returning a result gives the caller a value to use. It does not automatically update the variable supplied as an argument. To update that variable, the caller must assign the returned value to it.

Here, score receives the value of points when increment_score() is called. The function adds 1 to score and returns the new value. Compare what happens when the caller ignores that result and when it stores it:

def increment_score(score):
    score += 1
    return score

points = 42
increment_score(points)
print(points)
points = increment_score(points)
print(points)

After the first call, points is still 42: the function returned 43, but the caller did not store it. In the second call, points = increment_score(points) assigns that returned 43 to points.

The parameter score and the caller’s variable points are separate names. Reassigning score changes its value inside the function, leaving points unchanged. Chapter 15 explores where names are available and how this separation works.

14.10 Summary

A function names a reusable job. Parameters receive arguments, and return ends the call and sends a result to the caller. Printing only displays output; without an explicit return value, a call produces None. Check every expected path, and give the function a docstring that says what it does.

Decomposition connects smaller jobs into a program. By convention, a main function coordinates the program’s work. A main guard lets the file run directly while keeping its functions available for import. Each call has its own local names, so reassigning a parameter does not change the caller’s variable. The caller must store the returned result when it needs to keep it.

14.11 References and Further Reading

  • Python Tutorial: Defining Functions
  • Python Language Reference: Function Definitions
  • Python Library Reference: __main__
  • PEP 257: Docstring Conventions
  • Edsger W. Dijkstra: On the Nature of Computing Science (EWD 896)
  • Python Data Model: User-Defined Functions

15 Variable Scope and Constants

Quote

“[T]he complete meaning of a word is always contextual, and no study of meaning apart from a complete context can be taken seriously.”

J. R. Firth, The Technique of Semantics, p. 37, excerpt.

Dividing a program into functions separates the work, but it also separates the names used to do it. A variable created inside one function is not automatically available to the rest of the program. This is why Chapter 14’s functions used arguments and return values to exchange information.

Knowing where a name is available helps you decide where to keep a value. A calculation may need a value only during a function call, while a fixed discount rate may be useful throughout a module. This chapter explains those boundaries so you can follow how functions use and update values.

15.1 Local Names and Function Calls

Suppose a function calculates the total price for a purchase. It needs names for the price, the quantity, and the result of multiplying them. The caller needs the final value, but it does not need access to every name used along the way.

The scope of a name determines where in a program Python can use it. A parameter or a name assigned inside a function is a local variable. The name stays within the function’s local scope. In the example below, price, quantity, and subtotal all belong to the call to calculate_total():

def calculate_total(price, quantity):
    subtotal = price * quantity
    return subtotal

total = calculate_total(6, 4)
print(total)

The caller receives 24 and assigns it to total. The value has come back from the function, but the name subtotal remains local to the call. Adding this line below print(total) stops the program with a NameError:

print(subtotal)

Python cannot find subtotal outside calculate_total(), so the report ends with NameError: name 'subtotal' is not defined.

Each call has its own values for these local names. Another function can use names such as price or subtotal for its own work without changing the values in this call. That separation lets you understand a function’s calculation on its own.

A function you call cannot see the local names of the function that called it. In the following program, main() passes its total as an argument so that display_total() can use the value:

def display_total(total):
    print(f"Total: ${total}")

def main():
    total = 24
    display_total(total)

main()

There are two names spelled total: one in main() and one in display_total(). The argument passes the value between them. Their matching spelling is convenient, but it is not what connects them.

Try It Yourself

Try calling display_total() without passing the value from main():

  1. Remove total from the parameter list of display_total() and from the call in main(). Leave the print() unchanged.
  2. Predict whether the program will print a total, then run it. If an error occurs, look at the name it identifies.

15.1.1 Scope and Indented Blocks

You have also created names inside if statements and loops. Those blocks are indented, just like a function body, but they do not create separate scopes. A name assigned inside an if, while, or for block within a function still belongs to that function call.

This lets a decision or loop prepare a value for the statements that follow it. Here, the if statement chooses a label, and the function returns that label after the branches rejoin:

def length_label(text):
    if len(text) >= 8:
        label = "Long"
    else:
        label = "Short"
    return label

print(length_label("notebook"))
print(length_label("pen"))

Both branches assign the same local name, label. The return can use label even though it sits outside the if block.

Being in scope does not guarantee that a name has a value. An UnboundLocalError means Python tried to use a local name before that call had assigned it a value. Scope tells you where the name belongs; the path through the code determines whether an assignment has happened.

Try It Yourself

See what happens when only one branch assigns label in length_label():

  1. Remove the else line and its indented assignment, leaving return label in place.
  2. Predict what each of the two calls will do. Run the code and compare the output and any error message with your prediction.

15.2 Global Names and Constants

Local names keep each function’s work separate, but some values are useful to several functions. A fixed discount rate, for example, can sit at the top level of the module so those functions have one named setting to read.

A name assigned at the top level, outside any function, is a global variable. The following function receives a price through its parameter and reads the discount rate from a global name:

DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.10

def discounted_price(price):
    discount = price * DISCOUNT_RATE
    return price - discount

print(discounted_price(20))

DISCOUNT_RATE has global scope in this module. The parameter price and the calculated discount are local to each call of discounted_price(). A name assigned inside a top-level if statement or loop is global too, because those blocks do not create separate scopes.

A constant is a name the program intends not to reassign. The ALL_CAPS spelling communicates that intention to readers; Python does not enforce it. Constants usually appear after imports and before function definitions, so you can find the program’s fixed settings together.

When discounted_price() runs, Python looks up each name in this order:

Order Python looks in Example
First The call’s local names price and discount in discounted_price()
Then The module’s global names DISCOUNT_RATE
Finally The built-ins print

This lets discounted_price() read DISCOUNT_RATE without receiving it as an argument. It also raises a question: what happens if the function has a local name with the same spelling?

15.3 When One Name Hides Another

Using the same name in different scopes does not make it one shared variable. If a function assigns to a name that also exists globally, Python normally treats that name as local throughout the function. Inside that function, the local name hides the global one. This is called shadowing.

Follow the output before, during, and after display_x() to see whether its assignment changes the global x:

x = 5

def display_x():
    x = 9
    print(f"Inside display_x: {x}")

print(f"Before display_x: {x}")
display_x()
print(f"After display_x: {x}")

Before display_x: 5
Inside display_x: 9
After display_x: 5

The assignment changes only the local x. The repeated spelling can make this look like an update to one variable, but the function call and the module each have their own x.

Names can hide built-ins too. If you assign a value to print or str, later code in that scope will find your value instead of the built-in function. Choose names that describe your data and leave familiar function names available.

15.4 Keeping Changing Values Local

Shadowing can be especially confusing when you intend to update a value. In display_x(), the assignment supplies a new value directly. An update such as +=, however, needs to read the old value first. Consider this attempt to increase a global task count:

task_count = 2

def add_task():
    task_count += 1
    return task_count

print(add_task())

Running this program stops with an UnboundLocalError:

UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'task_count' where it is not associated with a value

The += update is an assignment, so Python treats task_count as local throughout add_task(). Adding 1 requires reading that local value first, but the call has not assigned it a starting value. The global value of 2 does not supply the missing local value.

You can avoid this confusion by making the exchange explicit. Let the caller keep the count, pass it to the function, and assign the returned result:

def add_task(task_count):
    return task_count + 1

def main():
    number_of_tasks = 2
    number_of_tasks = add_task(number_of_tasks)
    print(number_of_tasks)

main()

Now main() holds the count and decides when to update it. add_task() receives a starting value and returns the new one. Neither function needs access to the other’s local names, and neither name needs to be global.

Try It Yourself

Compare the printed count when main() keeps the returned value and when it discards it:

  1. Replace number_of_tasks = add_task(number_of_tasks) with just add_task(number_of_tasks).
  2. Predict the printed count, then run the program to check your prediction.
  3. Restore the assignment and run again to compare the two results.

Keeping a name within the part of the program that needs it is called minimizing scope. Here, the count changes in main(), so you know where to look for its updates. A global constant is useful for a fixed setting; a changing count is easier to follow when the code responsible for updating it keeps it locally.

15.5 Summary

Scope determines where Python can use a name. Parameters and names assigned inside a function are local, and each call has its own values for those names. Names assigned at the top level are global to the module. Arguments and return values let functions exchange information while keeping their local names separate.

Selection and loop blocks do not create separate scopes. A name assigned in one of those blocks remains part of the surrounding function or module, but the assignment must happen before you use it. Trying to read an unassigned local name raises UnboundLocalError, even when a global name has the same spelling.

Use ALL_CAPS for constants whose values the program intends not to change. Avoid accidental shadowing of global names or built-ins, and keep changing values local where possible. Passing values in and returning results makes it clear which part of the program is responsible for an update.

15.6 References and Further Reading

  • Python Tutorial: Scopes and Namespaces
  • Python Language Reference: Resolution of Names
  • PEP 8: Constants
  • J. R. Firth: The Technique of Semantics, p. 37

16 Errors and Assertions

Quote

Whatever you’re testing, you want it to fail early and you want it to fail spectacularly. Early success is a terrible teacher.

Chris Hadfield, address to research trainees at SickKids (2015).

Functions give you a smaller piece of a program to examine. You can follow an argument into a function, trace its operations, and compare the return value with what you expected. Chapters 14 and 15 explained how values move between calls; that understanding now helps you find mistakes.

Some mistakes stop a program with an error message. Others are quieter: the program runs to completion with a wrong answer, and nothing announces the problem. A loud failure is easier to investigate because its error report points to the failed instruction. A quiet one calls for the testing approach from Chapter 10, which compares actual results with the requirements. Assertions connect the two: they record an expected result as a condition the program checks, so a hidden mistake fails early and spectacularly instead of surviving in silence.

16.1 Understanding Error Reports

The examples follow a shop’s delivery rule: orders below $50 have a $5 fee; orders of $50 or more have free delivery. The function delivery_fee() receives an order total and returns the fee. Totals are non-negative integers representing whole dollars.

That rule establishes the expected result, regardless of how the function is written. A $30 order has a $5 fee, while a $70 order has a $0 fee. First, though, Python needs to execute the code that calculates it.

Each code example can run on its own. Several deliberately raise an error for you to examine. Browser reports may have different file labels and extra traceback entries compared with those shown here.

16.1.1 Syntax Errors

Before Python can run a file, its statements must follow the language’s grammar. A syntax error breaks those rules and prevents the file from executing. We have seen this kind of error already. The delivery-fee function illustrates how a small omission can cause it: the if header is missing the colon that introduces its indented body.

def delivery_fee(order_total):
    if order_total >= 50
        return 0
    return 5

print(delivery_fee(30))

Python reports SyntaxError: expected ':'.

Restoring the colon lets this example print 5. Even with valid syntax, an operation can still fail during execution.

16.1.2 Runtime Errors and Tracebacks

A runtime error occurs during execution. The function below has valid syntax, but main() passes the string "30". The comparison inside delivery_fee() needs a number:

def delivery_fee(order_total):
    if order_total >= 50:
        return 0
    return 5

def main():
    fee = delivery_fee("30")
    print(fee)

main()

Python raises an exception to signal the failure. Here, a TypeError reports that >= cannot compare a string with an integer. Execution stops before the function returns a fee.

The traceback shows the calls leading to the failure. For delivery.py, the report below omits full paths and expression underlining:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "delivery.py", line 10, in <module>
    main()
  File "delivery.py", line 7, in main
    fee = delivery_fee("30")
  File "delivery.py", line 2, in delivery_fee
    if order_total >= 50:
TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'

Read the traceback from the bottom up. The final line explains the TypeError; above it, line 2 identifies the failed comparison. Line 7 shows the call that passed "30", and line 10 shows the call to main().

Following the calls can reveal a mistake in an argument rather than in the failed operation. Here, the comparison is correct for a numeric total; the problem is the string supplied by main(). Changing "30" to 30 on line 7 lets the function return 5. Check both the failed operation and the values passed to it.

Try It Yourself

Can a statement before an error still execute? Compare the syntax-error and runtime-error examples above:

  1. Add print("Starting") as the first line of the syntax-error example. Predict whether the message will appear, then run it.
  2. Add the same line at the beginning of the runtime-error example. Predict what will appear, then run it and compare the results.
  3. What does the difference tell you about when Python detects each error?

16.2 When a Result Is Wrong

Once the code has valid syntax and receives a suitable argument, Python can carry out its instructions, and this time nothing will interrupt it. But executing the instructions is not the same as the instructions being right. Python knows nothing of the shop’s rule; whether the code expresses it is a question the interpreter cannot answer. This version uses > in its comparison:

def delivery_fee(order_total):
    if order_total > 50:
        return 0
    return 5

print(delivery_fee(30))
print(delivery_fee(50))
print(delivery_fee(70))

The output is:

5
5
0

For orders of $30 and $70, the fees agree with the rule, but an order of exactly $50 is charged incorrectly. A semantic error occurs when a program’s instructions produce behaviour that does not meet its requirements. Python performed the comparison correctly: 50 > 50 is false, so the function reaches return 5. The mistake is the choice of comparison. The rule includes $50 in free delivery, so the code needs >=.

This illustrates the connection between testing and debugging from Chapter 10. Testing reveals a mismatch between an expected result and an actual result. Debugging follows the execution that produced it to find the cause. Here, the particular input 50 makes the incorrect return path visible. Correcting the comparison and checking that input again establishes whether the repair addresses the problem.

16.3 Checking Results with Assertions

A later change could bring back the wrong fee at $50, even after you have repaired the comparison. Printing the fee still leaves you to judge it against the shop’s rule. An assertion records your expectation as a condition Python checks.

An assertion uses assert followed by a condition. A true condition lets execution continue silently; a false condition raises AssertionError. In this example, the comparison is repaired and the assertion checks the fee at $50:

def delivery_fee(order_total):
    if order_total >= 50:
        return 0
    return 5

assert delivery_fee(50) == 0
print("Check passed.")

Python calls delivery_fee(50) and compares its return value with 0. The condition is true, so the check passes and execution reaches the final print(). The assertion keeps the input and expected fee together, ready to check again when the code changes.

You can add a message after a comma to explain the expectation when an assertion fails. The following version uses the original > comparison again:

def delivery_fee(order_total):
    if order_total > 50:
        return 0
    return 5

assert delivery_fee(50) == 0, "Delivery should be free at $50"
print("Check passed.")

Because delivery_fee(50) returns 5, the assertion’s condition is false. The assertion’s message appears in the final line of the report:

AssertionError: Delivery should be free at $50

Although the function completed its calculation normally, the returned fee did not meet the expectation. Execution therefore stops at the assertion, before the final print(), and the traceback identifies the failed check.

Use assertions to check expectations about your code during development. Input validation handles unsuitable user values, for example by asking again inside a loop. That response belongs in the program’s ordinary if statements or loops.

Try It Yourself

Compare two ways a check can fail. Start with the example above, whose assertion includes a message:

  1. Run the code as written and keep its error report for comparison.
  2. Change > to >=. Predict whether "Check passed." will appear, then run the code to check the repair.
  3. Change the assertion’s call from delivery_fee(50) to delivery_fee("50"). Predict whether the error report will include the assertion’s message, then run it and compare the two failure reports.

16.4 Choosing Useful Test Cases

Passing the check at $50 tells you about that input alone. A function that always returned 0 would pass it, even though it would charge the wrong fee for smaller orders. A test case pairs an input with its expected result; choosing several cases lets you examine different parts of a function’s behaviour.

For the delivery rule, the important change occurs at $50. A boundary case lies at or beside that point. Checking just below, at, and just above the threshold examines both return paths and where the choice changes. Several large orders would all take the free-delivery path, leaving that transition untested.

Where do the expected results come from? From the shop’s rule, never from the function’s own calculation. A check that copies the function’s comparison repeats whatever mistake it contains, and the incorrect result passes. The example below includes checks at the threshold and just below it. Before running it, predict whether both assertions agree with the rule:

def delivery_fee(order_total):
    if order_total >= 50:
        return 0
    return 5

assert delivery_fee(50) == 0
assert delivery_fee(49) == 0
# Add another assertion here.
print("All checks passed.")
Try It Yourself

Use the shop’s rule to repair an expectation and extend the checks in the example above:

  1. Run the code. Identify the failed check and decide whether the function or its expected result needs changing. Correct it using the shop’s rule.
  2. Replace the placeholder comment with an assertion for a total just above $50. Work out the expected fee before running the code. Do all the checks pass?

16.5 From Individual Checks to a Test Suite

Even after a mistake is corrected, you can reuse the delivery-fee checks. A test suite is a collection of tests that you can run together. Rerunning the suite after a change checks both the behaviour you meant to alter and the behaviour that should stay the same.

When assertions run in one sequence, a failure stops execution before any later checks can run. A testing tool such as pytest runs checks in separate test functions and reports a result for each. Under its default settings, a failure ends the current test, while the remaining tests continue. You can therefore see which cases passed alongside those that failed.

That pattern of results can guide an investigation. If the case at $50 fails while those just below and above pass, the comparison at the threshold is a useful place to look. After a repair, rerunning the whole suite checks whether the correction fixed that case and left the others working.

Passing the suite means that the cases examined met their expectations. It does not show that every possible input works, so choosing useful cases remains important even with a testing tool. Writing and organizing your own pytest suites comes later.

16.6 Summary

A syntax error stops a file before it can run. A runtime error interrupts an operation during execution: the exception message explains the failure, and the traceback connects it to the calls that led there. A semantic error is the quiet one; the program runs normally and produces a result that does not meet the requirements.

An assertion records an expectation as a condition, turning a quiet mistake into a loud, early one. Test cases pair inputs with expected results, and those results come from the requirements, never from the function’s own code. Paths, boundaries, and limits help you choose useful cases. Assertions are development checks; required input validation stays in the program’s ordinary logic.

A test suite preserves cases for later changes, and pytest reports each test individually. Testing reveals mismatches; debugging investigates their causes. Both the implementation and the expected result have to agree with the requirements.

16.7 References and Further Reading

  • SickKids: Colonel Chris Hadfield Inspires SickKids Trainees to Reach for the Stars, the source of the opening quotation.
  • Python Tutorial: Errors and Exceptions, for syntax errors and reading exception reports.
  • Python Language Reference: The assert Statement, for assertion syntax and failure messages.
  • pytest: Get Started, for an introduction to separate tests and failure reports.

17 Lists and Slicing

Quote

“Data dominates. If you’ve chosen the right data structures and organized things well, the algorithms will almost always be self-evident.”

Rob Pike, Notes on Programming in C, Rule 5.
