As your programs handle more information, you need ways to keep related values together and process them as a group. A list lets you give a collection one name and work with its elements, even as its contents change.

The indexing and loops you know from strings carry over to lists, whose elements can be complete strings, numbers, or other values. You can add, replace, or remove elements, process the collection, and build new lists from selected or transformed values. An operation may change the existing list, return a value, or do both. Keeping those effects distinct helps you follow what your program does. Slicing lets you select the part of a sequence you need.

17.1 Keeping Related Values Together

A container keeps related values together so you can work with them as a group. One kind of container is a list, which stores its values in order. Each value in the list is called an element.

Suppose you are planning a walk from the harbour to the museum, then to the library and back to the harbour. You can record those stops with a list literal, a list written directly in your code. Square brackets ([]) enclose the elements, with commas between them:

stops = ["Harbour", "Museum", "Library", "Harbour"]
print(stops)
print(len(stops))

print(stops) displays the list, and len(stops) reports 4 because the route has four stops. The two "Harbour" elements record separate visits. A list keeps the order you give it, including repeated values; it does not automatically sort the names. If your plans change, you can add, remove, or replace stops.

Like a string, a list is a sequence: each element has a position you can select with an index. A for loop visits the elements in order, and each one is a complete place name rather than a single character.

You can check whether the route includes a place with a membership test. It checks for a whole element. "Museum" in stops is True because "Museum" is one of the stops. "Gallery" not in stops is also True because "Gallery" is absent.

[] creates an empty list, which could represent a route with no stops yet.

Closer Look

Every stop above is a string, but a list can hold any type of value, and Python even permits mixing types in one list. ["Harbour", 3, True] is a valid list.

17.2 Accessing and Replacing Elements

The indexing rules you know from strings also apply to lists. Index 0 selects the first element, and index -1 selects the last:

stops = ["Harbour", "Museum", "Library", "Station"]
print(stops[0])
print(stops[-1])
print(stops[len(stops) - 1])

The last two expressions select the same element: len(stops) - 1 is the last position, counted from the front rather than from the end. Each result is a complete string, rather than one of its characters. A list’s length counts elements, not the characters inside them.

An index must identify an existing position. Accessing one beyond the end raises IndexError, just as it does for a string. An empty list has no valid element index, including 0 and -1.

A list is mutable: operations can change its existing contents. To replace one stop, assign to its indexed position:

stops = ["Harbour", "Museum", "Library", "Harbour"]
stops[1] = "Gallery"
print(stops)

Assigning to stops[1] changes the existing list, replacing "Museum" with "Gallery" while keeping four stops. Assignment has the same rule as reading: the position must already exist, and a list does not grow to make room for a new one. An immutable string, by contrast, lets you read a character by index but not replace it this way.

Try It Yourself

In the replacement example above, change stops[1] to stops[4]. Predict what happens, then run it and inspect the report. Restore the original index afterward.

17.3 Adding and Removing Elements

A route may gain a new stop without losing an existing one. List methods can add values at the end or insert them between current elements:

stops = ["Harbour", "Museum"]
stops.append("Library")
print(stops)
stops.insert(1, "Gallery")
print(stops)
stops.extend(["Park", "Station"])
print(stops)

Each displayed route has grown. append() adds one element at the end. insert() places an element before the given position, shifting later elements along. extend() adds each item from another iterable, a value that a for loop can visit. Appending a list adds that whole list as one element; extending with it adds its elements separately.

A string is also iterable: a for loop over a string visits its characters one at a time.

Try It Yourself

In the route example above, replace only stops.extend(["Park", "Station"]) with stops.extend("Park"), dropping the square brackets. Predict the final list, then run it. Compare with a version that uses stops.append("Park") in that same position. Which call treats the name as one stop?

17.3.1 Removing by Value or by Position

Choose the removal operation according to what you know. remove() searches for a value and removes its first occurrence. pop() removes an element at a position and returns it; with no argument, it uses the final position:

stops = ["Harbour", "Gallery", "Museum", "Harbour"]
if "Harbour" in stops:
    stops.remove("Harbour")
print(stops)
last_stop = stops.pop()
print(last_stop)
print(stops)

The two calls remove different "Harbour" elements because remove() chooses by value and pop() by position. An absent value makes remove() raise ValueError, and pop() on an empty list raises IndexError, so the membership check comes first.

17.3.2 Changing a List and Returning a Value

Changing a list and returning a value are separate parts of a method’s behaviour. append(), extend(), insert(), and remove() change the list and return None. You can see both effects by keeping the result under a separate name:

stops = ["Harbour", "Museum"]
result = stops.append("Park")
print(stops)
print(result)

The list now includes "Park", but result is None. Assigning that result back with stops = stops.append("Park") would leave stops referring to None. When you only need the change, write stops.append("Park") as its own statement. By contrast, pop() also provides a useful result: the removed element.

17.4 Processing a List

A for loop can visit complete list elements just as it visited string characters. Use the element directly when the task does not require its index:

stops = ["Harbour", "Gallery", "Museum"]
for stop in stops:
    print(f"Next stop: {stop}")

Each pass assigns a complete string to stop, so the loop body can work with one route element at a time. A separate position counter would add no useful information here.

Calling stop.upper() inside this loop would produce a new string without replacing the element in stops. To keep transformed values, you can build a new list, as we will do shortly.

17.4.1 Totals and Extremes

Processing a collection may mean combining its values into one result. Suppose you want to know how busy a bicycle rack gets during the day, so you visit it four times and record how many bicycles are parked there each time. Each count is one observation, and the four observations make up the list:

counts = [6, 9, 4, 7]
print(sum(counts))
print(min(counts))
print(max(counts))

The results are 26, 4, and 9. sum() adds the values; min() and max() select the extremes. min() and max() need at least one element, while sum([]) is 0.

len(counts) counts the observations, and dividing the sum by that count gives the average. That calculation, like finding an extreme, needs a decision about what to do when there are no observations.

17.4.2 Checking for an Empty Collection

Before reporting a largest count, the program needs to know whether there are any observations. An empty list is false in a condition, and a non-empty list is true, so the list itself can provide the check:

counts = []

if counts:
    print(f"Largest count: {max(counts)}")
else:
    print("No observations recorded.")

For a list, if counts: asks the same emptiness question as if len(counts) > 0:. Here, the check keeps max() from running without an observation. The next chapter examines how values behave in conditions and how one check can protect another operation.

17.4.3 Counting Matches

Sometimes you need a count of only certain observations. As with counting characters in a word, an accumulator starts at 0 and the loop adds one whenever an observation passes the test. This function counts observations that meet a chosen minimum:

def count_busy_observations(counts, minimum):
    """
    Count the busy observations recorded at a bicycle rack.

    :param counts: a list of non-negative bicycle counts
    :param minimum: the smallest count considered busy
    :return: the number of busy observations
    """
    busy_count = 0
    for count in counts:
        if count >= minimum:
            busy_count += 1
    return busy_count

print(count_busy_observations([6, 9, 4, 7], 7))
print(count_busy_observations([], 7))

At a minimum of 7, the observations 9 and 7 qualify, so the first call returns 2. With an empty list, the loop makes no passes and the function returns the initial count of 0. In both cases, it reads the supplied list and returns a number without changing the list’s contents.

17.5 Building a New List

Counting matches gives you one number. When you need the matching values themselves, a list can collect them. Here, busy_counts starts empty and receives each qualifying observation:

counts = [6, 9, 4, 7]
busy_counts = []

for count in counts:
    if count >= 7:
        busy_counts.append(count)

print(busy_counts)
print(counts)

Selecting elements by a condition is filtering. The condition is a test each element either passes or fails, and the new list keeps only what passes. The loop visits counts from front to back, so the result [9, 7] contains the observations at or above 7, in their original order. Appending to busy_counts leaves counts unchanged, as the second output confirms.

Try It Yourself

In the filtering example, change >= 7 to > 7. Predict which observation will be affected, then check the result. Restore >= and choose one threshold that keeps every observation and another that keeps none. What does each case help you check?

You can check a filtered result with ==. Two lists compare equal with == when they contain equal elements in the same order. For example, [7, 9] == [9, 7] is False, even though both contain the same numbers.

You can also transform values instead of selecting them. If each bicycle count needs a correction of one, the new list can hold one adjusted value for every observation:

counts = [6, 9, 4, 7]
corrected = []

for count in counts:
    corrected.append(count + 1)

print(corrected)

The result is [7, 10, 5, 8]. This loop appends on every pass, so the new list has the same length as counts. Filtering can produce fewer elements; this transformation keeps one result per source element.

Both examples read one list and append to another. Adding or removing elements from the list you are currently traversing can shift positions and cause the loop to skip or revisit items. A separate result keeps the traversal stable while you select or transform values.

17.6 Sorting and Finding Values

The loops above leave counts in its original order. When you want to change a list’s order instead, sort() rearranges its elements into ascending order in place:

counts = [6, 9, 4, 7]
counts.sort()
print(counts)

The output is [4, 6, 7, 9]: the sorted values are in counts itself. Like append(), sort() changes the list and returns None, so write the call as its own statement. After sorting, counts records numerical order rather than the order of observations, so consider whether your program still needs the original sequence.

Sorting requires values that Python can compare. A list of integers or a list of strings works; mixing integers and strings raises TypeError, even though Python allows both types in the same list.

Other methods search or change a list’s contents. Treat each row below independently, with values starting as [6, 9, 6, 7] each time:

Operation Purpose Result or Change
values.count(6) Count occurrences of a value Returns 2
values.index(9) Find the first matching position Returns 1
values.reverse() Reverse the current order Changes the list to [7, 6, 9, 6]; returns None
values.clear() Remove all elements Changes the list to []; returns None

index() raises ValueError when the value is absent. Use membership when presence is all you need. Reversing is not the same as sorting into descending order: it flips whatever order the list currently has.

17.7 Taking a Slice

Indexing selects one element at a position. A slice selects a portion of a sequence. In sequence[start:stop], selection begins at start and ends before stop:

stops = ["Harbour", "Gallery", "Museum", "Park", "Station"]
middle = stops[1:4]
print(middle)

The result is ['Gallery', 'Museum', 'Park']. The highlighted positions show why stops[1:4] selects three elements:

Index 4 marks the first excluded element. This makes neighbouring slices fit together: stops[:2] ends before index 2, and stops[2:] begins there. Together they cover the route without gaps or overlap.

Omitting a bound uses the corresponding end of the sequence. Negative indexes count from the end, just as they do when selecting one element:

Slice Selected Elements
stops[:2] The first two
stops[2:] Everything from index 2 onward
stops[-2:] The final two
stops[:] All elements
stops[2:2] No elements ([])

Unlike a single out-of-range index, slice bounds beyond the ends are adjusted to the available sequence. With this route, stops[:20] includes all five elements. That is useful when asking for up to a certain number of items, but it can also hide an incorrect bound if you never inspect the result.

The optional third part, sequence[start:stop:step], supplies a step between selected positions. A positive step moves forward; a negative step moves backward:

stops = ["Harbour", "Gallery", "Museum", "Park", "Station"]
print(stops[::2])
print(stops[::-1])
print("Vancouver"[::2])

A step of 2 selects every second element: the stops at indexes 0, 2, and 4. A negative step selects backward, so with -1 the whole route comes out in reverse order. Strings are sequences too, so "Vancouver"[::2] works the same way. When the step is negative, omitted bounds adapt to the backward direction, so stops[::-1] alone is enough. A step of zero is invalid and raises ValueError.

In this example, change stops[::2] to stops[1::2]. Predict the selected stops before running. What changes when the step stays the same but its starting position changes?

17.7.1 A List Slice Creates a New List

Slicing does not shorten or reorder the source list. It produces a new list containing the selected elements:

stops = ["Harbour", "Gallery", "Museum", "Park"]
short_route = stops[:2]
short_route[0] = "Station"

print(short_route)
print(stops)

Replacing the first element of short_route affects the new list, while stops still begins with "Harbour". A full slice, stops[:], likewise creates a new list containing all the source elements.

Try It Yourself

In the short_route example, replace stops[:2] with stops[1:3]. Predict both output lines. Which source elements are selected, and which one does index 0 identify in the new list? Run the complete example with that one change.

17.8 Moving Between Text and Lists

Slicing selects text by position, but often the useful boundaries are spaces or other separators. With no argument, split() separates a string on runs of whitespace and returns a list of strings. join() combines string elements with a chosen separator:

request = "  sketch   paint  fold  "
words = request.split()
print(words)
print("/".join(words))

split() drops the whitespace at each end and treats repeated spaces as one separator, so words is ['sketch', 'paint', 'fold']. In "/".join(words), the string before the dot supplies the separator and the argument supplies the elements to combine.

Try It Yourself

In the request example above, change request.split() to request.split(" "). Predict both output lines before running. How does supplying a single-space separator affect repeated, leading, and trailing spaces?

17.9 Summary

Lists keep values in order, preserve duplicates, and let you change their contents. Indexing reads or replaces an element; methods add, remove, or rearrange elements. A method’s effect on the list and its returned value are separate, so consider both when using a call’s result.

Membership checks whether a complete element is present. Loops can combine list values into one result or build a new list by filtering and transforming them. An emptiness check protects operations that need at least one element. Slices select parts of a sequence using an exclusive stop and an optional step; slicing a list creates a new list. split() and join() connect lists with text processing.

17.10 References and Further Reading

  • Python Tutorial: More on Lists, for list methods and their return behaviour.
  • Python: Membership test operations, for checking whether an element is present.
  • Python: Common sequence operations, for indexing and slicing.
  • Python: String methods, including splitting and joining.

18 Boolean Logic in Depth

Quote

“Take care of the sense, and the sounds will take care of themselves.”

Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Chapter IX.

Working with lists gave you practical reasons to check before acting. A stop must be present before you remove it, and observations must be available before you find their maximum. Sometimes a decision needs several checks together: does a route have a first stop, and is that stop the harbour? You already know how to combine conditions with and, or, and not. Understanding how Python groups and evaluates those conditions lets you express the decision clearly and keep its operations safe.

A compound condition does more than produce an answer. An earlier check can make a later one unnecessary, so Python may skip an indexing operation or an entire function call. The order of those checks therefore matters. Choosing the question matters too: in tests for a substring, == compares complete values, and numbers that come from a calculation often need a tolerance rather than exact equality. In every case, the difference shows up in what a running program does.

18.1 Reading a Compound Condition

Suppose a community garden opens its greenhouse when a volunteer is present and either the weather is dry or the roof is closed. Naming each fact makes the rule easier to express. A Boolean expression produces a value like any other, so the whole condition is calculated and stored in can_open, rather than appearing as the test of an if:

volunteer_present = True
weather_dry = False
roof_closed = True

can_open = volunteer_present and (weather_dry or roof_closed)
print(can_open)

Either alternative is enough, but a volunteer must still be present. Parentheses keep those alternatives together, so and combines the volunteer requirement with their result.

Compound conditions follow the same precedence rules you met for arithmetic expressions. A comparison keeps its values together the way multiplication does. Among the Boolean operators, the order remains not, then and, then or. Without its parentheses, the greenhouse condition means (volunteer_present and weather_dry) or roof_closed.

Try It Yourself

Delete the parentheses from the can_open line and run the code again with the same values: the answer does not change. Now choose values for the three names that make the two versions disagree. Predict each result before you run it. Which greenhouse requirement does the version without parentheses fail to preserve?

Negation also depends on grouping. In not (weather_dry or roof_closed), Python answers the parenthesized question first and not flips that answer, so it is true only when the weather is not dry and the roof is not closed. Without the parentheses, not applies only to weather_dry, giving (not weather_dry) or roof_closed, true when the weather is not dry or the roof is closed.

18.2 Using Values in Conditions

The last chapter used if counts: to keep max() from running on an empty list, without comparing the list with True. Python’s truth value testing lets a condition use any value directly. An empty list is false, and so are numeric zero, False, and None. A non-empty value is true.

Strings follow the same rule: what matters is whether there is any content, not what the content says. A note left at a bicycle rack shows the difference:

note = ""

if note:
    print(f"Note: {note}")
else:
    print("No note was left.")
Try It Yourself

Change "" to "0". Predict the complete output, then run it. What is the difference between a note containing a zero and no note at all?

A check like this one often sits inside a compound condition, and there Python may not need to examine every part of it.

18.3 When Python Can Stop Evaluating

Grouping tells you which conditions belong together. Evaluation determines which parts Python actually needs to examine. Python evaluates the left operand of and or or first and tests its truth value. A false value lets and stop; a true value lets or stop. In either case, Python skips the right operand. This behaviour is short-circuit evaluation.

Expression Left Operand Is the Right Operand Evaluated?
left and right False No
left and right True Yes
left or right False Yes
left or right True No

Skipping an operand means skipping the operation it describes. A function call does not run, and an indexing operation does not attempt to select an element. This can change the program’s output, or make an error appear or disappear.

Watch Your Step

A call on the right of and or or may never execute. If an action must happen every time, give it its own statement instead of depending on its position in a condition.

18.3.1 Protecting an Operation

An empty route has no stop at index 0, and the last chapter showed that indexing an empty list raises an IndexError. The comparison is only safe when a stop exists, so check for a stop first. Short-circuit evaluation lets you put both checks inside one expression:

stops = []
starts_at_harbour = len(stops) > 0 and stops[0] == "Harbour"
print(starts_at_harbour)

With an empty route, len(stops) > 0 is false, so Python skips the indexing and assigns False. With a non-empty route, the check is true and Python compares stops[0] with "Harbour". A first stop makes the comparison possible, but that stop does not have to be the harbour.

The length comparison acts as a guard, a check that must pass before the operation it protects can run.

Try It Yourself

In the route example above, reverse the operands with stops still empty, and predict what happens before running, then read the error report. Next, try a non-empty route: why would testing only that route hide the problem? Restore the guard to the left afterward.

The same pattern protects max(), with the list itself as the guard:

counts = []
print(counts and max(counts) >= 8)

counts = [10, 7, 9]
print(counts and max(counts) >= 8)

and and or return one of their operands rather than always a Boolean, so the first answer is [] itself. Since [] is false, the expression still works in a condition. The route example printed False rather than [] because its guard was the comparison len(stops) > 0, which evaluates to False.

18.3.2 Observing a Skipped Call

A predicate function answers a yes-or-no question by returning True or False. A condition can ask its question by calling one. Short-circuit evaluation can skip that call just as it skipped the indexing in the route example. When it does, none of the function’s statements run. A temporary print() inside the function makes the skip visible. Here, a visitor may enter with a pass or a reservation:

def has_reservation(name):
    print("Checking the reservation")
    return name == "Noor"

has_pass = True
can_enter = has_pass or has_reservation("Noor")
print(can_enter)

Only one line appears: True. Checking the reservation never prints, because has_pass is True and or already has its answer; the call is skipped entirely. The final print() reports the answer to the whole condition. The missing message is the only sign that the reservation was never checked.

Try It Yourself

Change only has_pass to False. Predict both lines the example will display, then run it. Next, keep has_pass false and change the argument to "Eli". Predict before each run. Which change affects whether the function runs, and which affects the answer it returns?

18.4 Asking About Membership

You used in to check for a stop before removing it from a list. A membership test returns a Boolean answer: in tests for presence and not in tests for absence. What counts as a match depends on the collection:

print("tea" in ["tea", "juice", "water"])
print("tea" in ["teapot", "juice", "water"])
print("tea" in "teapot")

The results are True, False, and True. The first list contains the complete element "tea". The second has "teapot" instead, so its element test fails. Searching within the string "teapot" finds the consecutive substring "tea". List membership does not search inside each element.

Use == when you need equality between complete values and find() when you need a substring’s position or -1 for absence. Membership suits a yes-or-no question. All of these searches are case-sensitive. In the example, "tea" matched "teapot" because the cases match exactly. Searching for "Tea" instead would find nothing. When case should not matter, normalize the text first with .lower().

18.5 Comparing Approximate Numbers

Choosing the right comparison also matters for calculated numbers. You might expect 0.1 + 0.2 and 0.3 to compare equal:

total = 0.1 + 0.2
print(total)
print(total == 0.3)

Python prints 0.30000000000000004, and the comparison answers False. A floating-point number has limited precision: many decimal fractions have no exact finite binary representation, just as 1/31/31/3 has no finite decimal representation, only the endless 0.3‾0.\overline{3}0.3. Python stores a nearby representable value instead, and the difference from the intended value is representation error. The sum must fit the float format too, so Python rounds it to the nearest representable value. That second rounding is why the printed total carries extra digits.

Exact equality is a valid question, but for approximate calculations the useful one is whether the difference is small enough for the purpose.

18.5.1 Choosing a Tolerance

“Small enough for the purpose” needs a number. That number is a tolerance, the largest difference you will accept. Suppose a measured length must be within 0.01 metres of a two-metre target. The requirement sets a tolerance of 0.01 metres.

The math module provides math.isclose(), a predicate that reports whether two numbers are close enough:

import math

TOLERANCE = 0.01
target = 2.0
measured = 2.006

print(math.isclose(measured, target, rel_tol=0.0, abs_tol=TOLERANCE))

The result is True: 2.006 is about 0.006 metres from 2.0, inside the tolerance. In the call, abs_tol=TOLERANCE hands the function your tolerance. The rel_tol=0.0 argument switches off a second rule that allows a difference to grow with the size of the numbers. Your fixed tolerance is then the only test: an absolute tolerance, the same permitted difference whatever the target’s size.

Closer Look

The = in abs_tol=TOLERANCE does not assign a new variable. It passes a value to a named argument: the name before the = must match a parameter the function defines. The name does the matching instead of the position, so two named arguments can appear in either order.

18.6 Rounding a Value and Formatting Its Display

The failed comparison in the last section has a tempting repair: round both sides first.

print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2) == 0.3)

This prints True, but not because the numbers are close. Rounding each side to two digits compares what the values look like when displayed, not how far apart they are. A measured 2.008 metres is within the 0.01 metre tolerance of 2.0, but round(2.008, 2) is 2.01, so the rounded comparison rejects a measurement the requirement accepts. A tolerance states how close is close enough. Rounding to a number of digits cannot express it.

Rounding has other, real uses. round() returns a number with fewer digits: round(reading, 2) keeps two digits after the decimal point. The :.2f format produces text for display with exactly two digits after the decimal point:

reading = 1.204
rounded = round(reading, 2)
display = f"{reading:.2f}"

print(rounded, type(rounded))
print(display, type(display))
print(reading)

rounded prints as 1.2 and display as "1.20", but the difference is not the zero. Their types differ: rounded is a float you can use in another calculation, and display is a string meant for a reader. Neither operation changes reading, which still prints 1.204. As numbers, 1.20 and 1.2 are identical, so the zero is purely for presentation.

Rounding does not remove representation error. The rounded 1.2 is itself a decimal fraction with no exact binary representation, so it too is stored as a nearby value. Use a tolerance to express acceptable differences, rounding when a calculation needs fewer digits, and formatting when the reader needs a particular display.

18.7 Summary

Parentheses make the grouping of a compound condition clear. An empty list or string is false in a condition, and so are numeric zero, False, and None. Any other value is true. With and and or, short-circuit evaluation lets an earlier operand determine whether a later one is evaluated. Put each guard before the operation it protects, and remember that a skipped function call does not run at all.

Membership asks whether a substring or element is present. Equality compares complete values. Many decimal fractions have no exact binary representation, so == can report False for numbers that look equal. With approximate numbers, choose a tolerance from the requirement and compare with math.isclose(). Rounding produces a numeric result, while formatting produces text for display. Neither removes the representation error.

18.8 References and Further Reading

  • Python: Truth value testing, for values used directly in conditions.
  • Python: Boolean operations, including short-circuit behaviour and returned operands.
  • Python: Membership test operations, for strings and containers.
  • Python: Floating-point arithmetic, for representation error and its consequences.
  • Python: math.isclose(), for relative and absolute tolerances.
  • Python: round(), for rounding rules.

19 Ranges, Tuples, and Sets

Quote

“We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us.”

John M. Culkin, A Schoolman’s Guide to Marshall McLuhan, 1967.

Lists let you keep related values in order, preserve repeated items, and change a collection as your program runs. You can process those values with loops and use conditions to check whether an operation is appropriate. Those tools suit a changing route or a series of observations, but other problems call for a different kind of collection. A timer may mark every fifth minute, and a colour may hold its red, green, and blue values together.

Ranges, tuples, and sets express those needs in different ways. A range describes an integer progression, a tuple keeps values in fixed positions, and a set keeps distinct members without positional order. Loops and membership checks still work with all three, but each preserves different information and allows different changes. To choose among them, ask what the values mean and what your program will do with them.

19.1 Describing a Sequence with range()

Counting with a while loop requires both a condition and an update to the count. When you know the integer pattern in advance, a range can supply the values. It is an immutable sequence of integers described by a start, a stop value it does not include, and a step.

Compare these two ways to display the numbers from one through five:

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

for count in range(1, 6):
    print(count)

Both loops print 1 through 5. In the for loop, Python assigns each range value to count, so the body needs no separate update. The stop is 6 because, like a slice, a range excludes its stop value.

A counting pattern fits for with range(). A condition such as waiting for valid input fits while, because the number of passes depends on what happens during execution. The choice follows how the program knows whether more work remains.

19.1.1 Start, Stop, and Step

You can supply just a stop, both bounds, or both bounds and a step:

Form Meaning Example Values
range(stop) Start at 0, advance by 1 range(4): 0, 1, 2, 3
range(start, stop) Use the supplied start, advance by 1 range(2, 6): 2, 3, 4, 5
range(start, stop, step) Advance by the supplied step range(2, 9, 3): 2, 5, 8

For example, a timer can mark every fifth minute, including minute fifteen:

for minute in range(0, 16, 5):
    print(f"Minute {minute}")

Here, minute 15 is included because it falls before the stop of 16. The stop need not be a value in the progression. range(0, 20, 5) supplies the same markers because the next value after 15 would be 20, which the range excludes. A stop of 15 leaves out the final one.

A negative step counts downward:

for remaining in range(8, 0, -2):
    print(remaining)

The values are 8, 6, 4, and 2. Zero is excluded by the stop; including it would require a stop below zero. The step supplies the direction, so writing the larger bound first does not by itself make a range count downward.

Calling list() on a range creates a list of its values, making the progression easy to inspect in the REPL:

>>> list(range(8, 0, -2))
[8, 6, 4, 2]
Try It Yourself

Predict the values from range(3, 3), range(3, 0), and range(3, 0, -1), then use list() in the REPL to check. Which ranges are empty, and how do the start, stop, and direction explain the results?

An empty range is valid and gives a for loop no values to visit. A zero step raises ValueError. The arguments must be integers, so range(0, 1, 0.1) raises TypeError.

19.1.2 Working with a Range

A range describes a progression without storing every integer as a separate element. That is why displaying the range shows its description, while displaying a list made from it shows all the values:

markers = range(0, 16, 5)
print(markers)
print(list(markers))
print(len(markers))
print(markers[-1])
print(10 in markers)

The first two outputs are range(0, 16, 5) and [0, 5, 10, 15]. The remaining results, 4, 15, and True, show that a range supports length, indexing, and membership. Its values are fixed by the progression; append() and indexed assignment are unavailable.

A for loop can use the range directly. Converting it to a list is useful when you need to inspect all its values or create a collection you can change. For an existing list or string, you can usually visit its elements directly, as you did when processing lists.

19.2 Tuples for Values with Fixed Roles

A list often holds a changing number of similar items. Other groups have a fixed shape, with an agreed meaning for each position. A tuple is an immutable sequence, making it useful when those positions should stay fixed.

For example, an RGB colour has red, green, and blue components in that order:

colour = (32, 96, 160)
print(colour[0])
print(len(colour))

red, green, blue = colour
print(f"Red: {red}; green: {green}; blue: {blue}")

In red, green, blue = colour, unpacking assigns each element to its corresponding name. The first component becomes red, the second green, and the third blue. Those names express the roles more clearly than repeated indexes.

This form of unpacking requires the number of names to match the number of elements; two names here would raise ValueError. Unpacking works with lists too. Choosing a tuple for this colour is a design decision: it prevents the three component positions from being edited in place.

19.2.1 Immutability and Reassignment

Tuples support len(), indexing, membership, and slicing. Reading colour[0] is allowed, but assigning colour[0] = 64 raises TypeError. A tuple also has no append() method.

As with immutable strings, the name can still be assigned a new value:

colour = (32, 96, 160)
print(colour)

colour = (64, 96, 160)
print(colour)

The second assignment makes colour refer to a new tuple without modifying the first tuple’s contents.

19.2.2 Commas and Tuple Literals

The colour has three elements because that fits its purpose; Python permits tuples of other lengths too. Commas form a non-empty tuple, while parentheses make its boundaries clear. A single-element tuple therefore needs a trailing comma:

one_component = (32,)
one_number = (32)
print(type(one_component))
print(type(one_number))

The two types are tuple and int. Without the comma, (32) simply groups the integer 32. An empty tuple uses ().

19.2.3 Returning Related Results

A function returns one value, but that value can hold several related results. Here, a tuple keeps the smallest and largest readings together:

def measurement_limits(readings):
    """
    Find the smallest and largest readings.

    :param readings: a non-empty list of numeric readings
    :return: a tuple containing the minimum and maximum
    """
    return (min(readings), max(readings))

lowest, highest = measurement_limits([14, 11, 18, 13])
print(f"Lowest: {lowest}; highest: {highest}")

The caller receives (11, 18) and unpacks it into lowest and highest, producing Lowest: 11; highest: 18. The tuple’s order gives those values their meaning. Returning the minimum first is part of the function’s agreement with its caller, so the docstring states that order.

Try It Yourself

In the measurement example, reverse the two expressions inside the returned tuple, leaving the caller unchanged. Predict the output, then run it. Compare the original and reversed versions with a list containing just one reading. Which input reveals the wrong return order, and why? Restore the original return order afterward.

19.3 Sets for Unique Values

Lists and tuples preserve positions and repeated values. An inventory that needs only the kinds of plants available does not need either piece of information. A set is an unordered collection of distinct values. It can gather the plant names from several seed packets:

packets = ["basil", "mint", "basil", "thyme", "mint"]
plants = set(packets)

print(len(packets))
print(len(plants))
print("thyme" in plants)

The results are 5, 3, and True: five packets supply three distinct plant names, including thyme. Keeping each distinct value once is deduplication. Creating plants leaves the packets list unchanged, but the new set omits its repetitions and positions. From the set alone, you cannot recover how many packets of each plant you own.

Without positions, a set has no element at index 0 and cannot be sliced. You can iterate over its members, but your program should not depend on their display or iteration order. A set literal uses curly braces, as in {"basil", "mint", "thyme"}. To create an empty set, use set(); {} creates an empty dictionary.

Numbers and strings can be set members. Lists cannot: using [1, 2] as a member raises TypeError.

19.3.1 Adding and Removing Members

A set can gain or lose members after creation. add() inserts a member if it is absent; adding an existing member leaves the set unchanged:

plants = {"basil", "mint"}
plants.add("thyme")
plants.add("mint")
plants.remove("basil")

print(len(plants))
print("basil" in plants)

Only "mint" and "thyme" remain, so the output is 2 and False. Like the list methods you have used, these calls change the collection in place and return None.

For a set, remove() raises KeyError when the member is absent. discard() leaves the set unchanged in that case. The choice expresses an expectation: remove() makes a missing member visible as an error, while discard() accepts that it may already be absent. clear() removes every member.

Try It Yourself

In the example above, change the removal to plants.remove("sage"). Predict what happens, then run it and inspect the report. Replace only remove with discard and predict the two output lines before running again. What does each version assume about whether the member must be present?

A set uses the values Python receives, so "Mint" and "mint" remain different strings. If those spellings should describe the same plant, normalize the text before gathering distinct names. Deduplication alone cannot repair inconsistent data.

19.4 Choosing a Representation

The packet list records individual packets; the plant set records distinct plant names. You can keep both when you need both kinds of information. Several collections may hold the same values. Choose one that makes their meaning clear and supports the operations you need:

Requirement Collection Reason
Keep an editable route List Preserves positions and repeated stops
Count in regular steps Range Describes start, stop, and step
Pair a minimum and maximum Tuple Fixed roles; elements cannot be replaced
Keep distinct plant names Set Records each name once

19.5 Summary

Ranges describe integer progressions using a start, exclusive stop, and non-zero step. A for loop can visit their values directly, and the stop follows the same exclusion rule as slicing.

Tuples keep elements in fixed positions and let you unpack related values into meaningful names. A function can return one tuple containing several results, with their order forming part of its agreement with the caller. Sets keep distinct members without positional order, supporting membership checks and deduplication. Choose a representation according to the information and operations your program needs.

19.6 References and Further Reading

  • Python: Ranges, for progression rules and supported sequence operations.
  • Python Tutorial: Tuples and Sequences, for construction and unpacking.
  • Python: Set Types, for membership and mutation.
